course: Daily Bread Sales: Bakery Production System

lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
Bread is not just food; it is a daily cash machine. In almost every African community, from Lagos to Nairobi to Accra, people buy bread every single day. Unlike a wedding cake or a birthday cake, bread is bought by the same customers over and over. That means if you bake good bread, you don't need to find new customers every day. You just need to keep your regulars happy.

Think about your own street. How many people eat bread for breakfast? How many buy it on the way to work? How many send children to the shop for a loaf in the evening? In many areas, a small bakery can sell 200 to 500 loaves a day. At a profit of 50 to 100 naira per loaf, that is 10,000 to 50,000 naira profit daily. That is real money.

But why do some bakeries fail? They fail because they treat bread as a side business. They bake when they feel like it. They don't measure. They don't keep records. They don't show up. The bakery business is a daily business. Your customers expect bread today, tomorrow, and the next day. If you miss a day, they will buy from someone else. If you miss a week, they will forget you.

This module will teach you the foundation: why bread is daily cash, what tools you need, how to bake step by step, common mistakes, safety, and a practical exercise. By the end, you will understand that bread is not just a productâit is a system. A system of buying ingredients, mixing, baking, and selling every day. When you master the system, you can feed your family, pay school fees, and even employ others.

Start thinking like a baker, not a hobbyist. Your oven is your ATM. Your ingredients are your investment. Your customers are your daily income. Let's begin.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To start a small bakery, you don't need a million naira. You need the right tools and materials. Here is what you need for a basic daily bread production of 50 to 100 loaves.

First, the oven. A gas oven is best for consistent heat. A single-deck gas oven can cost 150,000 to 300,000 naira. If that is too much, you can start with a charcoal oven or even a local mud oven. But gas is cleaner and easier to control. You also need baking trays. Get at least 10 trays so you can bake in batches. Each tray holds about 6 to 8 loaves.

Next, mixing tools. You need a large mixing bowl or a dough mixer. A 20-litre bowl is good for small batches. A hand mixer or a wooden spoon for mixing. You also need a weighing scale. This is not optional. Bread requires exact measurements. A digital scale that measures up to 5 kg is fine. You need measuring spoons and cups for yeast, salt, and sugar.

Ingredients: flour, yeast, salt, sugar, water, and oil or butter. For 50 loaves, you need about 25 kg of flour, 250 g of yeast, 500 g of salt, 1 kg of sugar, and 2 litres of oil. You also need waterâclean water. And you need packaging: bread bags, twist ties, and a marker to write dates.

Other tools: a dough scraper, a rolling pin (if you make shaped bread), a cooling rack, and a storage bin for flour. You also need a table for shaping and a clean apron and hairnet. Don't forget a fire extinguisher and a first aid kit.

You can buy these tools gradually. Start with the oven, trays, scale, and basic ingredients. As you grow, add a mixer and more trays. The key is to start. Many successful bakers started with one oven and one tray. What matters is that you have the essentials to bake consistently.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Baking bread is a science, but it is also simple. Follow these steps for a basic white bread recipe that makes 10 loaves.

Step 1: Gather and measure. For 10 loaves, you need 5 kg of flour, 50 g of yeast, 100 g of salt, 200 g of sugar, 2.5 litres of warm water, and 100 ml of oil. Use your scale. Don't guess.

Step 2: Activate the yeast. In a small bowl, mix yeast, sugar, and 1 cup of warm water (not hot, or it will kill the yeast). Let it sit for 10 minutes until it foams. This tells you the yeast is alive.

Step 3: Mix the dough. In a large bowl, put flour and salt. Make a well in the center. Pour in the yeast mixture, remaining water, and oil. Mix with your hands or a spoon until a sticky dough forms.

Step 4: Knead. Turn the dough onto a floured table. Knead for 10 to 15 minutes. Push, fold, turn, repeat. The dough should become smooth and elastic. If it sticks, add a little flour. If it's too dry, add a little water.

Step 5: First rise. Put the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with a damp cloth, and let it rise in a warm place for 1 to 2 hours. It should double in size.

Step 6: Punch down and shape. Punch the dough to release air. Divide into 10 equal pieces. Shape each into a loaf and place in greased loaf pans.

Step 7: Second rise. Cover and let rise again for 30 to 45 minutes.

Step 8: Bake. Preheat oven to 200Â°C (400Â°F). Bake for 25 to 30 minutes until golden brown. The bottom should sound hollow when tapped.

Step 9: Cool and package. Remove from pans and cool on a rack. Once cool, bag and label with date. Sell same day for best quality.

Remember, consistency is key. Use the same recipe, same measurements, same oven temperature. That way, your customers get the same great bread every day.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Even experienced bakers make mistakes. Here are the most common ones and how to fix them.

Mistake 1: Yeast not foaming. You mix yeast with water and nothing happens. Fix: Your water was too hot (above 45Â°C) or too cold, or the yeast is expired. Use lukewarm water and check the expiry date. Always proof your yeast before mixing.

Mistake 2: Dough too dry or too sticky. You add too much flour or too little water. Fix: Measure accurately. If dough is sticky, add flour one tablespoon at a time. If dry, add water one tablespoon at a time. Don't dump.

Mistake 3: Bread doesn't rise. The dough stays flat. Fix: Your yeast was old, water too hot, or room too cold. Use fresh yeast, warm water, and let it rise in a warm place (like near the oven or in a closed cupboard).

Mistake 4: Bread is dense and heavy. Fix: You didn't knead enough or didn't let it rise long enough. Knead for at least 10 minutes and give it the full rising time. Also, check your flourâold flour can cause dense bread.

Mistake 5: Bread burns outside, raw inside. Fix: Oven too hot. Reduce temperature to 180Â°C and bake longer. Use an oven thermometer to check actual temperature.

Mistake 6: Bread tastes bland. Fix: You forgot salt or used too little. Salt is not just for taste; it controls yeast. Use the right amount.

Mistake 7: Inconsistent sizes. Fix: Use a scale to divide dough into equal pieces. Customers notice when one loaf is smaller.

Mistake 8: Selling stale bread. Fix: Bake daily. If you have leftovers, sell them as day-old at a discount or make breadcrumbs. Never sell stale bread as fresh.

Mistake 9: Poor packaging. Fix: Use clean bags, tie them well, and label with date. Presentation matters.

Mistake 10: Not keeping records. Fix: Write down how much flour you used, how many loaves you sold, and your profit. This helps you improve and grow.

Learn from these mistakes. Every mistake is a lesson. Fix them and your bread will be better, and your customers will keep coming back.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Safety in the bakery is not just about avoiding accidents; it is about producing clean, safe bread that won't make your customers sick. Here are the key safety and best practices.

Personal hygiene: Always wash your hands with soap before handling dough. Wear a clean apron, hairnet, and if possible, gloves. Tie back long hair. Don't bake if you are sick, especially with cough, cold, or stomach issues. Cover any cuts with a waterproof bandage.

Clean workspace: Keep your tables, tools, and floor clean. Wash mixing bowls, trays, and utensils after every use. Use food-safe sanitizer. Don't let raw dough sit on surfaces for hours. Clean up spills immediately to avoid slips.

Food safety: Store flour in a dry, cool place in sealed containers. Keep yeast in the fridge or a cool dark place. Check expiry dates on all ingredients. Don't use mouldy flour or expired yeast. Use clean water. Don't mix old dough with new dough unless you know what you're doing (some bakers use old dough as a starter, but it must be handled properly).

Oven safety: Gas ovens can leak. Check for gas smells. Never light an oven with a match if you smell gas. Use the built-in igniter or a long lighter. Keep flammable items away from the oven. Use oven mitts when handling hot trays. Have a fire extinguisher nearby and know how to use it.

Knife and tool safety: Keep knives sharp; dull knives slip. Cut away from your body. Store knives safely. Don't leave tools on the floor.

Best practices for quality: Measure accurately. Use a thermometer to check water temperature (35-40Â°C for yeast). Keep a baking log: date, time, temperature, and results. This helps you repeat success. Cool bread completely before packaging to prevent sweating and mould. Label with date and price. Rotate stock: sell older bread first.

Customer safety: Never sell bread that is burnt, undercooked, or dropped on the floor. If in doubt, throw it out. Your reputation is your business. A single case of food poisoning can destroy your bakery.

Finally, train your workers. Everyone who touches dough must know these rules. Safety is a habit. Make it part of your daily routine.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
Now it's time to put what you've learned into practice. This exercise will help you understand your local market and plan your daily bread business.

Exercise 1: Market survey. Visit 5 shops or bakeries near you that sell bread. Ask: How many loaves do you sell per day? What is your selling price? What size are the loaves? What time do customers buy the most? Write down your findings. This tells you the demand and the going price.

Exercise 2: Cost calculation. Using the recipe from Lesson 3 (10 loaves), find the current prices of flour, yeast, salt, sugar, oil, and gas/electricity. Calculate the total cost. Divide by 10 to get cost per loaf. Now compare with the selling price you found. What is your profit per loaf? If profit is less than 30% of selling price, you need to adjustâmaybe buy in bulk or reduce waste.

Exercise 3: Bake a test batch. If you have access to an oven, bake 10 loaves using the step-by-step method. If you don't have an oven, find a local bakery and ask to watch or assist for a day. Note the steps, the timing, and the challenges. Write down what you would do differently.

Exercise 4: Identify your customers. Who will buy your bread? Will you sell from home, supply shops, or go door-to-door? List 10 potential customers or shops. Talk to them. Ask if they would buy from you if you supplied fresh bread daily. Get their phone numbers.

Exercise 5: Create a daily plan. Write a schedule: what time you wake up, mix dough, bake, cool, package, and sell. Include time for cleaning and record-keeping. A sample: 4am start, 4:30 mix, 5:30 shape, 6:30 bake, 7:30 cool, 8am sell. Adjust to your market.

Exercise 6: Set a goal. How many loaves do you want to sell daily in one month? Write it down. Then write the steps to get there: buy tools, practice, find customers, etc.

Do these exercises before moving to Module 2. They will give you a real foundation. Remember, a business plan on paper is good, but action is better. Start small, learn fast, and grow daily.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Why Bread Is Daily Cash

In most African neighbourhoods, bread is not a luxury item â it is a daily necessity. From Lagos to Nairobi, from Accra to Kampala, bread appears on breakfast tables, in lunch packs, and in evening tea sessions. For a small bakery or a home-based baker, this daily demand is the foundation of a reliable cash business. Unlike cakes that depend on events, or snacks that compete with many alternatives, bread sells every single day. This practical reference module gives you the tools, numbers, and methods to turn that daily demand into consistent profit.

This lesson is written for the RISE AFRICA Skills learner who wants to run a bakery as a business, not just as a hobby. Every table, checklist, and diagram below is designed to help you make faster, smarter decisions with your money and your time.

Why Daily Bread Equals Daily Cash

Bread has three business advantages that few other food products share:

  1. High frequency: People buy bread daily or every few days. This means your cash register rings every day, not once a month.
  2. Low unit cost: A loaf of bread is affordable to almost every household, so your customer base is large.
  3. Short production cycle: From mixing to selling, a simple bread batch takes 3â5 hours. You can bake, sell, and repeat the same day.

In many African cities, the informal bread market is dominated by small bakeries and roadside vendors. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), bread and bakery products are among the most consumed processed foods in sub-Saharan Africa, with demand growing alongside urbanisation (FAO, 2021). This is not a niche â it is a mass market.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING: Fire and Burn Hazards in Bread Baking

Baking involves high temperatures (200â250Â°C), open flames, hot ovens, and hot baking tins. In many African bakeries, firewood or charcoal ovens are used, which increases the risk of burns, fires, and smoke inhalation. Always keep a fire extinguisher or sand bucket nearby. Never leave the oven unattended. Use thick, dry cloth or heat-resistant gloves when handling hot tins. Ensure proper ventilation to avoid carbon monoxide poisoning. Keep children and untrained helpers away from the oven area. If you use gas, check for leaks with soapy water before lighting. A single fire can destroy your entire business and endanger lives â safety is not optional.

Step-by-Step Method: From Dough to Daily Cash

  1. Plan your daily batch: Decide how many loaves you will bake based on yesterday's sales. Start with 50â100 loaves if you are new.
  2. Weigh ingredients accurately: Use a scale. Inaccurate measurements cause inconsistent bread and waste.
  3. Mix and knead: Combine flour, yeast, salt, sugar, oil, and water. Knead for 10â15 minutes until the dough is smooth and elastic.
  4. First proof: Cover the dough and let it rise in a warm place for 1â2 hours until doubled in size.
  5. Shape and second proof: Divide, shape into loaves, place in greased tins, and proof for 30â60 minutes.
  6. Bake: Preheat oven to 200â220Â°C. Bake for 25â35 minutes until golden brown and hollow-sounding when tapped.
  7. Cool and pack: Cool on racks for at least 30 minutes before packing to prevent soggy bread.
  8. Sell and record: Sell the same day. Record every sale and every expense in a notebook or phone app.

Common Mistakes and Fixes

  • Mistake: Baking too many loaves and having leftovers. Fix: Track daily sales for one week and bake only what you can sell.
  • Mistake: Using expired yeast. Fix: Check expiry dates and store yeast in a cool, dry place.
  • Mistake: Not recording costs. Fix: Use a simple cash book. Know your cost per loaf.
  • Mistake: Selling on credit. Fix: Encourage cash sales. If you must give credit, keep a strict ledger and follow up.
  • Mistake: Ignoring hygiene. Fix: Wash hands, clean surfaces, and cover dough. Customers buy with their eyes first.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Keep a daily cash book â record every sale and expense.
  • â Store flour, yeast, and sugar in dry, sealed containers.
  • â Check oven temperature with a thermometer if possible.
  • â Cool bread completely before packing.
  • â Keep fire safety equipment within reach.
  • â Reinvest a portion of daily profit into tomorrow's ingredients.

quiz.q: Why is bread considered 'daily cash'?
options: A) It is expensive to make.
B) People buy it every day.
C) It lasts for many weeks.
quiz.explanation: Bread is a daily staple, so customers buy it repeatedly, providing consistent daily income.

quiz.q: What is a key reason some bakeries fail?
options: C) They have too many customers.
quiz.explanation: Consistent measurement is crucial for quality and repeat business; without it, bread quality varies and customers leave.

quiz.q: What is the recommended oven type for a small bakery?
quiz.explanation: Gas ovens provide consistent heat and are easier to control for daily baking.

quiz.q: Why is a weighing scale important in bread making?
options: A) To weigh the final bread for selling
C) To check if the dough is ready
quiz.explanation: Bread requires exact measurements for consistency; guessing leads to poor results.

quiz.q: How much profit can a small bakery make daily if it sells 200 loaves at 50 naira profit per loaf?
quiz.explanation: 200 loaves Ã 50 naira profit = 10,000 naira daily profit.

quiz.q: What should you do before mixing yeast with water?
quiz.explanation: Expired yeast will not activate, so always check the date before use.

quiz.q: What is the correct water temperature for activating yeast?
quiz.explanation: Lukewarm water activates yeast without killing it; hot water kills yeast.

quiz.q: How long should you knead dough for basic bread?
quiz.explanation: Kneading for 10-15 minutes develops gluten, making the dough smooth and elastic.

quiz.q: What should you do after the first rise?
quiz.explanation: Punching down releases air, and shaping prepares the dough for the second rise.

quiz.q: What is a sign that bread is fully baked?
options: B) It sounds hollow when tapped on the bottom
quiz.explanation: A hollow sound indicates the bread is cooked through.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when dough doesn't rise?
quiz.explanation: Expired yeast or water that is too hot or cold prevents rising.

quiz.q: How can you fix bread that is dense and heavy?
options: B) Knead longer and allow full rising time
quiz.explanation: Dense bread often results from under-kneading or insufficient rising; more kneading and time help.

quiz.q: What should you do if bread burns outside but is raw inside?
options: B) Reduce oven temperature and bake longer
quiz.explanation: Lowering the temperature allows the inside to cook without burning the outside.

quiz.q: Why is salt important in bread dough?
options: B) It controls yeast and adds taste
C) It makes bread rise faster
D) It preserves bread for weeks
quiz.explanation: Salt enhances flavor and regulates yeast activity.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for packaging bread?
options: B) Label with date and price
quiz.explanation: Labeling helps with stock rotation and customer trust.

quiz.q: Why should you keep records in a bakery?
options: B) To track profit and improve
quiz.explanation: Records help you understand costs, sales, and where to improve.

quiz.q: What is the first step in personal hygiene for bakers?
quiz.explanation: Handwashing prevents contamination of dough.

quiz.q: How should flour be stored?
options: A) In an open bag on the floor
B) In a sealed container in a cool, dry place
quiz.explanation: Proper storage prevents moisture, pests, and spoilage.

quiz.q: What safety equipment should be near the oven?
quiz.explanation: A fire extinguisher is essential for gas oven safety.

quiz.q: Why should you cool bread completely before packaging?
options: A) To make it easier to slice
B) To prevent sweating and mould
quiz.explanation: Cooling prevents condensation inside the bag, which causes mould.

quiz.q: What is a best practice for selling bread?
options: A) Sell stale bread as fresh
B) Rotate stock and sell older bread first
D) Keep bread in the sun
quiz.explanation: Stock rotation ensures freshness and reduces waste.

quiz.q: What should you do if you drop a loaf on the floor?
options: A) Dust it off and sell
C) Give it to a child
quiz.explanation: Food safety requires discarding dropped bread to avoid contamination.

quiz.q: Why is a market survey important before starting a bakery?
options: B) To know demand and pricing
quiz.explanation: Understanding demand and prices helps you plan profitably.

quiz.q: How can you calculate cost per loaf?
options: A) Divide total ingredient cost by number of loaves
quiz.explanation: Cost per loaf is total cost divided by loaves produced.

quiz.q: What is a good daily plan for a baker?
options: B) Start early morning and follow a schedule
C) Bake only when you feel like it
quiz.explanation: Consistent daily routine ensures bread is ready for customers.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a test batch?
options: B) To practice and identify issues
quiz.explanation: Test batches help you learn and improve before full production.

quiz.q: How many loaves does the recipe in Lesson 3 make?
quiz.explanation: The recipe yields 10 loaves.

quiz.q: What is the second rise time for the bread recipe?
quiz.explanation: After shaping, the dough needs 30-45 minutes for the second rise.

quiz.q: What temperature should the oven be for baking bread?
quiz.explanation: 200Â°C (400Â°F) is standard for baking bread.

quiz.q: What is a key benefit of selling bread daily?
options: B) You build a loyal customer base
D) You can charge any price
quiz.explanation: Daily sales create regular customers who rely on you.
